Sup A: bolton_2006_intermediate_standard_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Intermediate-standard blocking)
The Intermediate-standard blocking model represents protein fouling of microporous membranes by combining intermediate blocking, which reduces the available pore area, with standard blocking, which constricts pores and raises filtration resistance. Based on Darcy’s law, it predicts filtrate volume over time during constant-pressure filtration and pressure rise over time during constant-flow filtration using two fitted parameters. The paper tested it on human IgG filtration through a 0.22 μm PVDF membrane and BSA filtration through a virus-retention membrane, including constant-pressure and constant-flow runs. Model curves were fitted to measured filtration profiles by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. In the tested cases, this combined model did not improve on the relevant individual blocking model, and the authors describe it as applicable when the combined mechanisms match observed fouling.
comparison: The earlier Ho and Zydney (2000) model used three fitted parameters and required numerical integration for volume- or pressure-time predictions.
comparison: The paper cites Grace (1956) for standard-blocking background and Hermia (1982) for standard, complete, and intermediate blocking laws.
comparison: The paper compares its combined models with the more physically detailed combined blockage-and-cake model of Ho and Zydney (2000), noting that the new models are simpler to implement.
equipment: Constant-pressure filtration was performed in 13 or 47 mm stainless-steel membrane holders supplied from pressure vessels.
experiments: Five constant-pressure BSA runs used Viresolve 180 in 47 mm holders and continued until flux fell 98% from its initial value of 3.58 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
experiments: The constant-flow IgG experiments used a flux of 579 L/m² h through 47 mm Durapore membrane samples.
experiments: Three constant-pressure IgG experiments used 13 mm holders and continued until flux fell 95% from its initial value of 1.13 × 10⁻³ m/s.
feed: The BSA feed was prepared at 2.5 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS.
feed: The human plasma IgG feed was prepared at 10.0 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS.
fitting: For constant-pressure IgG, the paper fitted one of the three experimental data sets and reported that the other two were similar.
fitting: Model fits were compared by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between measured data and model predictions.
formulation: The combined fouling models were derived from Darcy’s law.
formulation: The combined model reduces to its component individual models when one mechanism dominates.
measurement: Filtrate mass was collected on an electronic balance with a load cell connected to a computer data-acquisition board.
measurement: The BSA filtration results were averaged across five runs, with standard deviations calculated at each time point.
measurement: The constant-pressure setup recorded data every second for one hour.
mechanisms: In the combined model, intermediate blocking reduces available membrane area while standard blocking increases filtration resistance.
mechanisms: Intermediate blocking represents some particles sealing pores while other deposited particles accumulate on top of them.
mechanisms: Standard blocking represents deposits constricting straight cylindrical membrane pores.
membrane: The BSA virus-filtration tests used Viresolve 180, a PVDF composite with a thin ultraporous layer over a thicker microporous layer.
membrane: The IgG sterile-filtration tests used 0.22 μm nominal-pore-size Durapore PVDF membranes.
model: Intermediate-standard blocking is one of the five combined fouling models developed in the paper.
model: The model is expressed through algebraic time relationships rather than a state-based dynamic system.
operation: Constant-pressure tests used 10 psi for Durapore membranes and 30 psi for Viresolve 180 membranes.
parameters: The model uses two fitted parameters, the intermediate-blocking constant and the standard-blocking constant.
prediction: The model predicts permeate volume over time for constant-pressure operation and pressure over time for constant-flow operation.
results: For constant-flow IgG, the intermediate-standard model fitted as well as the intermediate-blocking model alone.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the intermediate-standard model produced the same fit as the intermediate-blocking model alone.
results: For constant-pressure IgG, the intermediate-standard model fitted no better than the standard-blocking model alone.
scope: The authors say the combined models involving standard blocking do not cover as broad a range of flux-decline behavior as the cake-complete model.
scope: The paper presents the combined standard-and-intermediate equations as applicable when fouling is observed to involve that specific combination of mechanisms.
use: The authors position intermediate-standard blocking as a candidate for describing fouling when the combined mechanisms agree with experimental observations, rather than as a broadly useful general-purpose fit.
validation: The paper reports fitting the model to experimental profiles but does not describe a separate held-out validation data set.

Sup B: nopens_2004 · PBM AND ACTIVATED SLUDGE FLOCCULATION: FROM EXPERIMENTAL DATA TO A CALIBRATED MODEL
The Aggregation-breakage PBM models how activated sludge flocs change in size during flocculation. It predicts the floc size distribution over time, representing aggregation between flocs and breakage of larger flocs. The model is a one-dimensional population balance that is discretized into size classes and solved using the moving pivot method. It was calibrated using online laser-diffraction measurements from flocculation experiments at two mixing intensities, with several distribution measures tried as fitting targets. The authors recommend fitting the number distribution for applications involving gravitational solid-liquid separation, while concluding that the model needs more flexibility to describe the measurements adequately.
application: The authors recommend fitting the number distribution for gravitational solid-liquid separation because small flocs are problematic in wastewater treatment.
calibration: Calibration compared four fitting targets: volume-percent distribution, D[4,3], number distribution, and weighted number distribution.
calibration: For weighted-number fitting, measurement variances and weights were calculated using a multinomial counting-error assumption.
calibration: Parameter estimation used weighted least squares in WEST.
calibration: The paper reports point estimates but does not provide confidence intervals or other measures of parameter uncertainty.
data: The initial condition for the population balance is the measured initial number distribution.
data: The two calibration datasets were obtained from Biggs & Lant 2000, who studied the effect of mixing intensity on flocculation kinetics.
equipment: Floc size distributions were measured online with a Malvern Mastersizer E using laser light diffraction and a flow-through cell.
equipment: The flow-through cell flow rate was set to 3 ml/s to reduce shear effects and pump-pulsation influences and approximate isokinetic sampling.
measurement: The laser-diffraction measurements require dilution below 0.2 g/L and assume that the particles are spherical.
mechanisms: Aggregation is represented with a Smoluchowski population-balance model combining collision frequency and collision efficiency.
mechanisms: Breakage is represented by a size-dependent breakage rate from Spicer & Pratsinis 1996, with a breakage-rate coefficient estimated during calibration.
mechanisms: Collision efficiency is treated as a constant between zero and one.
mechanisms: The collision-frequency description was taken from Spicer & Pratsinis 1996 and relates collisions to floc properties and mixing conditions.
numerics: In a comparison on the same data, the fixed pivot method predicted a lower zeroth moment and more flocs in larger size classes than the moving pivot method.
numerics: The authors recommend the moving pivot discretization, which they implemented alongside the fixed pivot method in WEST.
numerics: The fixed pivot method led to an aggregation-parameter estimate about 50% lower than the moving pivot method, which the authors regarded as erroneous.
numerics: The moving pivot recommendation follows Kumar & Ramkrishna 1996, whose comparison with an analytical solution found better predictions than the fixed pivot method, including on a coarse grid.
operation: The data came from reflocculation experiments run at average velocity gradients of 19.4 and 37.0 s⁻¹.
operation: The model is used for relatively short flocculation experiments, with a maximum duration of 4 h.
parameters: Two aggregation and breakage parameters were estimated: the collision efficiency and the breakage-rate coefficient.
performance: Fits to volume-based targets described the middle of the volume distribution, roughly 35–350 μm, better than the distribution tails.
performance: Fitting the number distribution reduced small-tail underprediction to about 1.5–2.5, although the predicted volume distribution was poor.
performance: The authors concluded that the model lacks flexibility to describe the measured distributions adequately.
performance: Volume-percent fitting underpredicted the small-size number classes by factors of about 10–15, while D[4,3] fitting underpredicted them by about 15–30.
performance: Weighted-number fitting gave small-tail underpredictions of about 2–3.3.
prior work: The calibration methodology extends earlier activated-sludge flocculation PBM work by Nopens et al. 2002 and Biggs & Lant 2000.
prior work: The model draws on the Smoluchowski framework described by Ramkrishna 2000 and uses aggregation and breakage descriptions from Spicer & Pratsinis 1996.
prior work: The paper compares its discretization approach with Kumar & Ramkrishna 1996 and notes that Biggs & Lant 2000 used the Hounslow et al. 1988 discretization.
structure: Discretization converts the population balance into a finite set of ordinary differential equations, one for each size class.
structure: The model is dynamic and segregates biomass into a one-dimensional distribution of floc sizes rather than representing it as a single lumped sludge concentration.
structure: The paper does not report the number of size classes used, so the total number of distribution states cannot be determined from its description.
structure: The size distribution is expressed in numbers of flocs per unit volume, with floc size represented as volume.
system: The experimental sludge flocs were sonicated into single cells of about 1 μm and microcolonies of about 10 μm before being allowed to reflocculate.
system: The model represents flocculation of activated sludge, the particle-aggregation process involved in the liquid-solid separation stage of wastewater treatment.
transformation: For the volume-to-number conversion calculations, the paper used a biomass concentration of 3 g/L and density values of 1, 1.04, and 1.7 g/cm³.
transformation: The authors converted volume fractions to number concentrations using an estimate of total floc volume and assuming spherical flocs.
transformation: The authors found that the earlier log-normal-distribution transformation used by Biggs & Lant 2000 introduced large errors in the resulting number distributions.
transformation: The new grid-transformation method preserved the mass mean diameter D[4,3] of the original distribution.
transformation: To transfer the measurements to a model grid, the authors interpolated the cumulative volume distribution at the pivots of the new grid and then calculated the volume fractions.
validation: The reported comparisons use the two calibration datasets; the paper does not report an independent validation dataset.

answer.summary: A models protein fouling during membrane filtration, whereas B models activated-sludge floc aggregation and breakage; their systems and mechanisms are distinct.
